title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Fabrication | MPI (US)
description: On-site magnetic particle inspection for US fabricators: weld toes, lugs, structural joints and tank attachments to AWS D1.1 and ASME. Request an MT quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Fabrication and Welding in the United States
html:
Magnetic particle inspection (MPI, or mag particle testing) finds cracks and other flaws at or just below the surface of ferromagnetic welds and parts. Atlantis NDT sends technicians to fabricators in the United States to examine weld toes, fillet welds, attachment welds, lifting lugs and heavy structural joints to AWS D1.1, ASME and API requirements. We report each indication with its location and accept or reject status. For a scoped quotation, request an MT inspection quote with your weld list.

Why fabricators use magnetic particle inspection

Most weld cracking in carbon and low-alloy steel starts at the surface or very close to it: toe cracks, crater cracks, hydrogen cracks in the heat-affected zone, and cracks that open up during or after post-weld heat treatment. A magnetic particle examination is fast, tolerant of mill scale left after grinding, and shows the indication in place on the part, which is why it is the working method on the fabrication floor. A technician can examine a fillet weld on a lifting lug in minutes, mark the indication and hand the weld back to the welder for repair.

That speed has a limit. MT sees only what is on or near the surface; the volume of a groove weld is the job of ultrasonic testing, and non-magnetic alloys need a different surface method. Matching method to joint is part of every scope we write, and the pages for ultrasonic testing in fabrication and penetrant testing in fabrication show where each sibling method takes over.

The fabrication work we examine

MT scopes in a fabrication shop follow the product:

  • Structural steel: fillet and groove welds on beams, columns, base plates and connection details, examined under AWS D1.1 where the contract or engineer requires it. Our structural steel MPI page covers erection-site work in more detail.
  • Pressure vessels: nozzle-to-shell welds, support lugs and saddles, internal attachments and weld repair areas on carbon and low-alloy vessels built to ASME Section VIII, with the examination technique taken from ASME Section V Article 7.
  • Piping spools: branch connections and socket or fillet welds on ferromagnetic material where ASME B31.3 requires or the owner specifies magnetic particle examination.
  • Tanks: shell-to-bottom corner welds, nozzle reinforcement pads and temporary attachment scars on API 650 tanks, where the standard calls for surface examination of selected welds.
  • Lifting and handling: lifting lugs, padeyes, spreader beams and shackles made in the shop, covered by our MPI of lifting equipment page.

Codes, and who decides what is acceptable

The code names the method and fixes the acceptance limits. In fabrication that usually means AWS D1.1 for structures, ASME Section VIII for vessels, ASME B31.3 for process piping and API 650 for tanks, with the examination procedure written against ASME Section V Article 7 and the practice described in ASTM E709. Our explanation of the article is in ASME Section V Article 7 explained.

Acceptance is the code's job, applied by whoever the contract names. We measure and report: relevant indications are classed by shape and size, and the report states which criterion was used. A technician does not repair or waive anything. If the fabricator wants an indication dressed out by grinding and re-examined, that re-examination is recorded against the same weld number.

Technique details that matter on the shop floor

Magnetic particle inspection looks simple, and that is why bad examinations are common. A valid one controls the variables the procedure names.

  • Field direction: a crack shows best when it lies across the magnetic field. Each area is examined twice with the field in two roughly perpendicular directions, so cracks of any orientation are tested.
  • Yokes and lifting power: portable electromagnetic yokes are checked against a test weight before use, with the yoke leg spacing set to the procedure. Prods can arc and burn the surface of a part, so many fabrication specifications restrict or prohibit them on pressure parts and high-strength steel.
  • Particles: visible dry or wet particles in a contrasting color for ordinary shop lighting; fluorescent particles under ultraviolet light for higher sensitivity, which needs a darkened work area and a black light whose intensity is measured at the surface.
  • Surface condition: heavy scale, weld spatter and thick paint reduce sensitivity. Procedures set what must be removed first, and thin coatings are tolerated only if the procedure was demonstrated for them.
  • Field strength verification: a pie gauge or a flux indicator confirms that the field is strong enough at the part, and the report records the check.
  • Demagnetization: parts that will be machined, coated or put in service near sensitive equipment may need demagnetization when the specification asks for it.

Our broader weld-focused page, magnetic particle weld inspection, goes through this in sequence for root, hot-pass and final-weld checks.

What MT finds in fabricated welds and what it misses

On a clean ground surface, MT reliably shows toe cracks, crater cracks, lack of sidewall fusion that breaks the surface, and surface-open porosity or undercut in the form of indications that a technician evaluates against the code. It also detects near-surface flaws on ferromagnetic steel, to a depth that depends on field strength and flaw size.

It does not examine non-magnetic materials such as austenitic stainless steel or aluminum, it does not size the depth of a crack, and it tells you nothing about internal slag or incomplete penetration deep in a thick joint. When any of those matter, the scope should add UT or a penetrant method. Our comparison of MT and PT is a short guide to choosing between the two surface methods.

What the MT report contains

Typical contents of a fabrication MT report
ItemWhat we record
ComponentJob number, drawing, weld or part identification, material and joint type
ProcedureProcedure number and revision, code and edition, acceptance standard
MethodYoke, prod or coil, AC or DC, wet or dry, visible or fluorescent, and the lighting level used
VerificationYoke lifting test, field indicator check, particle and contrast check
PersonnelTechnician and qualification level under the written practice, with the Level III approving the procedure
FindingsLocation and length of each indication, type, accept or reject, and a sketch or photograph where required

Why a magnetic particle examination gets rejected as a procedure

Sometimes the welds are fine and the examination is not. Auditors and owner inspectors reject MT records for reasons that have nothing to do with the metal: no recorded yoke lifting test, a missing particle concentration check on wet suspensions, a procedure revision that does not match the code edition on the drawing, or an ultraviolet light whose intensity was never measured at the part. A record that lacks the field direction used on each area cannot show that both directions were covered. We build the report so those items are captured at the time of the examination, not reconstructed afterward.

Timing causes the other category of problem. Examining a weld before it has cooled, before the code-required delay for hydrogen-sensitive steel, or before grinding has cleared the surface produces either an unreliable examination or a false clear. If the weld sequence is tight, tell us which passes need interim examination, such as a root or hot pass on a thick joint, and we will plan the visits around the welders instead of behind them. Where examination happens after post-weld heat treatment, the report states that, because cracks that open in heat treatment are among the findings owners care about most.

What to send for a quote

  • The code or specification, with edition and acceptance criteria
  • Weld list or drawing marks for the joints to examine, with the percentage required
  • Material grade, thickness and whether the part is ferromagnetic throughout
  • Surface condition, coating and weld stage, such as as-welded, ground or after heat treatment
  • Whether a fluorescent method is called for, and the availability of a darkened area
  • Witness points and who must be present at each hold point
  • Shop or yard address, badging requirements and any hot-work or confined-space permits

Planning on the fabrication floor

MT fits between the weld-out and the next operation, so the plan should tie examinations to hold points rather than to a calendar. Welds are usually ready for MT once they have cooled and been ground or cleaned to the procedure's surface requirement. For hydrogen-sensitive steel the code may require examination after a delay following welding; that delay is part of the contract and we plan around it rather than shortcut it. Parts that are painted or galvanized before examination are a recurring source of rework, so say early if the paint schedule is fixed.

Technicians are mobilized to your shop for the agreed scope, with their own yoke, particles, gauges and light meter. If a darkened area is needed for fluorescent work, a curtain or a booth is arranged with you in advance. Written procedures can be supplied by us under Level III review: see NDT technical procedure development.

Training your fabrication QC staff

If you prefer to keep routine MT in-house, we train your people through MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, and the magnetic particle simulator gives them yoke and field-direction practice before they touch production welds. The employer, not the course provider, issues the personnel qualification under SNT-TC-1A. Industry-wide context is in NDT training for manufacturing.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and specialist techniques sit outside this page. Our crews do not weld, grind or repair, and we do not select the examination percentage; that comes from the code and the contract. MT is limited to ferromagnetic material: for stainless steel and aluminum we use the penetrant method. For the national picture see magnetic particle testing and the complete MT guide.

faq.q: Can MT be used on stainless steel pressure vessels?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steel is non-magnetic, so magnetic particle inspection will not work on it. Duplex and martensitic grades behave differently, but for ordinary austenitic vessels the surface method is liquid penetrant, which is covered on our penetrant fabrication page.

faq.q: Do you use prods on pressure parts?
faq.a: Only when the procedure and the specification allow it. Prods can arc and burn the surface, so many fabrication specifications restrict them on pressure parts and high-strength steel, and we default to yokes unless the contract directs otherwise.

faq.q: Who decides whether an MT indication is acceptable?
faq.a: The code and the party named in the contract decide, not the technician. We report each indication with location, length and type, state which criterion was applied, and the owner, its inspector or the fabricator's quality manager accepts or rejects.

faq.q: Is fluorescent MT better than visible particles?
faq.a: Fluorescent particles are more sensitive but need a darkened area and a controlled ultraviolet light. Visible contrast particles work in ordinary shop lighting. The procedure and customer specification set which one applies, and we confirm that before mobilizing.

faq.q: Do I need to grind welds before MT?
faq.a: Usually the surface must be free of spatter, loose scale and heavy paint, and some specifications require grinding flush. Mill scale on a clean weld may be acceptable if the procedure was demonstrated for it, so confirm the condition with us before the crew travels.

faq.q: What do you need to quote a fabrication MT scope?
faq.a: Send the code and edition, the weld list or drawing marks, material and thickness, surface and coating condition, any fluorescent requirement, witness points and the site address with access and badging details. A written procedure speeds the quote, though we can supply one.

faq.q: Do you examine lifting lugs and padeyes?
faq.a: Yes. Lugs, padeyes and below-the-hook devices are common MT jobs, examined to the owner's program, the manufacturer or the relevant ASME B30 standard. See our page on magnetic particle inspection of lifting equipment for the full detail.

faq.q: Does MT replace UT on groove welds?
faq.a: No. MT shows surface and near-surface flaws, while UT examines through the thickness of the weld. Many AWS D1.1 and ASME scopes call for both, and we recommend the combination after reading your drawings and code requirements.

When the specification requires it, parts are demagnetized after examination and the residual field is checked with a gauge. Not every job needs this; machining, plating, coating and proximity to instruments are the usual reasons it is asked for.
